passages.t: Raised with Christ: set your minds above
passages.happening:
“Therefore, since you have been raised with Christ, strive for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things” (verses 1-2).

“For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory” (verses 3-4).
passages.hearers:
Here the letter turns, as Ephesians does at 4:1. Everything before was about who Christ is and what believers have in him. Now comes how to live.

The new teaching also told people to look ‘up’, to seek visions of heaven and to climb higher by rules and self-denial. Paul says: yes, look up, but look to Christ, who is already there, seated at God's right hand. You do not climb to heaven by your own effort. You were raised there with him.

‘Set your minds’ means more than thinking about heaven. It means letting what is true about Christ shape your choices, your loves and your fears here.

Notice verse 3. ‘You died.’ The old life is over. ‘Your life is now hidden with Christ in God.’ Hidden means safe, kept where no one can steal it, and also not yet seen. People cannot always see what God is doing in a believer. But one day, when Christ appears, it will be seen.

This is not a call to ignore the world. The next verses are about anger, lies, family and work. Minds set on things above live better down here.
passages.ot:
‘Seated at the right hand of God’ is Psalm 110, the psalm the New Testament quotes more than once of Christ's rising and reign: “The LORD said to my Lord: ‘Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet’” (Psalm 110:1).

And the life hidden in God is what the psalmist hoped for: “Whom have I in heaven but You? And on earth I desire no one besides You” (Psalm 73:25).
passages.asks: Paul says your life is hidden with Christ. Ask what your mind is set on, most of the day. Ask whether you are trying to reach God by effort, or living from the place he has already given you. And ask what would change this week if you believed that your real life is safe with Christ.

passages.happening:
“Put to death, therefore, the components of your earthly nature: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires, and greed, which is idolatry” (verse 5). Because of these, God's judgment is coming (verse 6), and “When you lived among them, you also used to walk in these ways” (verse 7).

“But now you must put aside all such things as these: anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language from your lips. Do not lie to one another, since you have taken off the old self with its practices, and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator” (verses 8-10).

“Here there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free, but Christ is all and is in all” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
‘Put to death’ is strong. Paul does not say ‘manage’ these things, or ‘cut down’. Because believers have died with Christ, they are to treat the old ways as dead too.

The first list is about desire: sexual sin, and greed, which Paul calls idolatry because it treats money or things as if they were God. In the cities the readers knew, sex outside marriage, especially for men, was widely accepted. These were not rare crimes. They were ordinary life. Paul says, ‘you also used to walk in these ways’. He does not look down on them. He reminds them where they came from.

The second list is about words and temper: anger, rage, malice, slander, foul talk, lies. These are the sins that wreck a church. Notice they come right after sexual sin and greed. Paul does not let anyone think the sins of the tongue are small.

The picture is clothes again: take off the old self, put on the new. And the new self is being renewed ‘in the image of its Creator’. God is restoring in his people the likeness he made them for.

Verse 11 lists the divisions of that world. Greeks and Jews; the circumcised and not; ‘barbarians’, a Greek word for anyone who did not speak Greek; Scythians, peoples from north of the Black Sea whom Greeks thought the roughest of all; slaves and free. In Christ none of these makes anyone better or worse. ‘Christ is all and is in all.’
passages.ot:
God made human beings in his image: “So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). The new self is that image being renewed.

God promised a new heart to people whose hearts had turned hard: “I will remove their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 11:19).

And Israel's law already broke down the wall between native and foreigner in love: “So you also must love the foreigner, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 10:19).
passages.asks: Paul names sins of desire and sins of the tongue side by side. Ask which list you are more likely to excuse in yourself. Ask what ‘put to death’ would mean for one habit you know well. And ask which of the old divisions, of race, class, language or politics, still decides how you treat people.

passages.t: Put on the new self, and over everything, love
passages.happening:
“Therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity” (verses 12-14).

“Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, for to this you were called as members of one body. And be thankful” (verse 15). “Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God” (verse 16).

“And whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through Him” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Notice the order. First Paul tells them who they are: ‘the elect of God, holy and beloved’. Then he tells them what to wear. They do not become loved by putting on kindness. They put on kindness because they are loved.

The five virtues are all about other people: compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience. And then the two hardest: bear with one another, and forgive. The measure of forgiveness is high: ‘as the Lord forgave you’.

Love is the last garment, worn over all the rest, like a belt or an outer coat that holds everything together. Without love, the virtues fall apart.

‘Rule’ in verse 15 is a word for an umpire who decides a contest. When believers disagree, let the peace of Christ make the call.

And notice how much this passage says about the church together: one body, teaching one another, singing together, giving thanks. Three times Paul mentions thankfulness in three verses. A thankful church is hard to divide.

Verse 17 takes all of life in. Not only worship on Sunday, but ‘whatever you do, in word or deed’. Every ordinary thing can be done in Jesus' name.
passages.ot:
The virtues Paul names are God's own character, as he showed it to Moses: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). God's people are to look like him.

The law said, “Do not seek revenge or bear a grudge against any of your people, but love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18).

And Israel's worship was full of song and thanks: “Come, let us sing for joy to the LORD” and “Let us enter His presence with thanksgiving” (Psalm 95:1-2).
passages.hard:
‘Forgive as the Lord forgave you.’ Does this mean a person who has been badly hurt must act as if nothing happened, or go back to someone who is still hurting them?

No. Forgiveness lets go of revenge. It is not the same as trusting someone again, and it does not mean a crime should go unreported or that anyone should stay in danger. A person can forgive and still keep a safe distance, still tell the truth about what happened, and still seek justice through the proper authorities. Forgiveness can take time, and it is not a switch. The site's notes on Matthew 18 and Luke 17 say more.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.

If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true. Tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul tells you to put on love over everything. Ask whom you find hardest to bear with, and what it would look like to be patient with them this week. Ask whether there is a complaint you have been holding on to. And try doing one ordinary task today, deliberately, in the name of the Lord Jesus, with thanks.

passages.t: Wives and husbands, in the Lord
passages.happening:
Paul turns to the household. “Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord” (verse 18).

“Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
These two verses are short, and they sit inside the household passage that runs to 4:1. Ephesians 5:21-33 says the same things at greater length, and should be read alongside them.

The first hearers lived in Roman households, where by law and custom the father of the house held great power over his wife, children and slaves. Writers on running a household spoke to the man about how to rule. Paul speaks to wives directly, as people who answer to the Lord for themselves. And what he asks of them is set ‘in the Lord’: it is fitting as part of following Christ, and it can never require what Christ forbids.

Then Paul speaks to husbands, and he does not tell them to rule. He tells them to love, and not to be harsh, bitter or cruel. In a world where a husband's power at home was large, that command put a limit on it.

Much is agreed by Christians who read these verses differently. The husband is to love, and never to be harsh. Paul never tells a husband to make his wife submit. He speaks that word to wives themselves, so ‘submit’ is never a husband's to demand or enforce. Husband and wife stand before Christ as equal members of his body. And nothing here gives anyone a licence to control, frighten or harm another person.
passages.ot:
God made man and woman together in his image: “in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27). Both bear his likeness, and neither owns the other.

The prophets called marriage a covenant of faithfulness: Malachi speaks of “your companion and your wife by covenant” (Malachi 2:14).

And Proverbs knows what harsh words do: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1).
passages.hard:
Christians agree on much here, as ‘What the first hearers would catch’ sets out above. They differ on what ‘submit’ asks of a marriage today. These notes do not choose. The site's chapter note on Colossians 3, and the plain note on Ephesians 5:21-33, set out both readings; here they are in short, each as its own holders would put it.

Complementarians hold that men and women are equal in dignity and worth but given different callings in marriage. They read these verses, with Ephesians 5, as teaching a lasting pattern: the husband leads in self-giving love, as Christ leads the church, and the wife freely gives her submission, never something taken. They insist that the husband's calling is the heavier one, and that headship never licenses harshness or control, as verse 19 itself says.

Egalitarians hold that men and women are equal in dignity and in calling. They read Paul as working inside the household of his day while changing it from within, as with slavery in the verses that follow, and they read Ephesians 5:21, ‘Submit to one another’, as the key to the whole household passage. They believe the direction of the gospel, seen in verse 11 of this chapter and in Galatians 3:28, points to marriages of mutual submission.

Both are held by Christians who honour Scripture. It is a question that divides faithful churches, not the faith.

Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. If you are in an abusive marriage, seek safety first. Talk to a pastor or a counselor you trust, or call a local domestic violence line. These notes are not legal advice.

If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true. Tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul tells husbands, ‘do not be harsh’. If you are married, ask whether your words at home are gentle or harsh, and what your spouse would say. Ask what it means for your marriage to be ‘in the Lord’. And whoever you are, ask whether the homes you know are places where everyone is safe.

passages.happening:
“Children, obey your parents in everything, for this is pleasing to the Lord” (verse 20).

“Fathers, do not provoke your children, so they will not become discouraged” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
As in Ephesians 6, Paul speaks to children directly. The letter was read aloud in church, and they were listening. They are members of the church, and their obedience is something that pleases the Lord.

In a Roman household a father held legal power over his children as long as he lived, and harsh discipline was common. Paul puts a limit on that power. Do not provoke them. Do not keep pushing, nagging, belittling or punishing until they give up.

And notice the reason: ‘so they will not become discouraged’. The word means losing heart, the spirit going out of a child. Paul cares about how children feel inside, not only about how they behave. A father's job is not only to be obeyed. It is to raise a child who does not lose heart.
passages.ot:
Paul's words to children rest on the fifth commandment: “Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land” (Exodus 20:12).

Proverbs gives both parents a voice in a child's life: “Listen, my son, to your father’s instruction, and do not forsake the teaching of your mother” (Proverbs 1:8).

And the God who is a Father to his people is “compassionate and gracious, slow to anger” (Exodus 34:6). Earthly fathers are to reflect him.
passages.hard:
‘Obey your parents in everything.’ Does this mean a child must obey whatever a parent says?

No. Paul's reason is ‘for this is pleasing to the Lord’. A child's obedience belongs to the Lord first, and no parent can command what the Lord forbids. In Ephesians 6:1 Paul says the same in other words: ‘obey your parents in the Lord’. And the very next verse limits the parent: do not provoke your children. These verses describe a home where a parent's authority is held under God and used for the child's good.

These words must never be used against a child who is being harmed. No one may use ‘obey your parents’ to keep a child quiet about abuse, or to send a child back to someone who is hurting them.

Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: If you are young, ask what it would look like to please the Lord in how you treat your parents. If you are a parent, ask whether anything in your home is wearing down your child's heart: harshness, constant criticism, broken promises, or never having time. Ask what would help your child not to lose heart.

passages.happening:
“Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything, not only to please them while they are watching, but with sincerity of heart and fear of the Lord” (verse 22).

“Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord and not for men, because you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving” (verses 23-24).

“Whoever does wrong will be repaid for his wrong, and there is no favoritism” (verse 25). The words to masters follow in 4:1.
passages.hearers:
Slaves were a large part of the people in Roman cities, and many households, including some in the church, had them. People became slaves through war, debt, birth or being abandoned as babies. Roman slavery was not based on race. Some slaves held skilled posts and could hope to be freed; many lived hard lives under the full legal power of their masters, who could buy, sell and beat them.

This is the longest part of the household passage, and it is spoken to the slaves. They were in the room when the letter was read, as members of the church. Paul tells them that their work is seen by the Lord, and that they will receive ‘an inheritance’. By law a slave was property, not an heir. Paul says these slaves are heirs of God.

‘There is no favoritism’ cuts both ways. A slave who does wrong will answer for it, and so will a master, as the next verse says. Before God, the owner gets no special treatment.

Notice too the letter's setting. Onesimus, a slave from Colossae, carried this letter back with Tychicus (4:9), and Paul sent with him the short letter to Philemon, asking his master to receive him “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16).
passages.ot:
Israel's law told masters, “You are not to rule over them harshly, but you shall fear your God” (Leviticus 25:43), and to pay a poor worker “each day before sunset, because he is poor and depends on them” (Deuteronomy 24:15).

Job knew that master and servant were made by the same God: “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?” (Job 31:15).

And the God of Israel shows “no partiality” (Deuteronomy 10:17).
passages.hard:
Why does Paul tell slaves to obey, instead of condemning slavery? Paul does not command the end of slavery here, and that should not be softened. He writes to a small, powerless movement in an empire where slavery was everywhere and slave revolts were crushed with great violence.

But within that world he does what ordinary household rules did not. He speaks to slaves as people who answer to God and will inherit from him. He tells masters, in the next verse, to give their slaves ‘what is right and fair’, because they too have a Master. He says that in Christ there is no ‘slave, or free’ (verse 11). And in the letter carried with this one he asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother. Many readers see in this the seeds of the truth that would undo slavery: every person bears God's image, and in Christ there is neither slave nor free.

The history of these verses is painful. In the Atlantic slave trade and in the American South, slaveholders and many preachers used verses like these to demand obedience from enslaved Africans and to defend slavery as biblical, while they ignored the words to masters and the equality of all in Christ. That was a misuse, and it was wrong. Atlantic slavery, built on race and kidnapping, was very different from the Roman kind, and the law of Moses punished kidnapping with death. Christians who opposed slavery drew on the same Bible. The church's record was mixed, and it must be named honestly.

Nor are these verses a simple rule for employment today. A worker is not property, and a boss is not an owner. Some of what Paul says, to work honestly and with your whole heart, can be applied to work with care. But no one should use these verses to demand silence about mistreatment at work.

The note on Ephesians 6:5-9 and the Honest Answer ‘Why didn't the Bible just ban slavery?’ say more.
passages.asks: Paul says, ‘It is the Lord Christ you are serving’. Ask whether you work only when someone is watching. Ask whom you treat as beneath you because of the work they do. And if you have power over others, ask whether you remember that the Lord shows no favouritism.
